cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and TRI clones
processing: Fully oxidised orthodox black tea in broken and leaf grades; the mid-country's warmer climate gives a bigger leaf and a darker, fuller cup than the high-grown districts.
harvest_season: Year-round and fairly even; the first quarter of the year tends to be best.
appearance_dry: Dark brown, neatly made broken leaf or longer leaf grades.
taste_profile: Full and smooth with a mild briskness, light malt and a touch of sweetness; the most milk-friendly of the Ceylon districts.

brewing.notes: Four minutes, milk if you like; leaf grades give a second steep.

vintage_note: Sold through the Colombo auction by estate and grade year-round with no sharp quality season; a good deal goes into blends and tea bags, with some estate lots sold on their own. Not an ageing tea: use within a year or so of manufacture.
description:
Kandy, the old royal capital in the middle of Sri Lanka, is where the island's tea industry began in the 1860s, when James Taylor planted the first commercial field at Loolecondera shortly before leaf rust wiped out the coffee that the planters had relied on. The district's gardens sit at roughly 600 to 1,200 metres, 'mid-grown' in trade language, and they make a fuller, darker, rounder tea than the high districts above them.

Manufacture is orthodox, mostly broken grades with some leaf grades, in the standard Ceylon pattern of wither, roll, quick oxidation and firing. The warmer climate grows bigger leaf and produces a deeper, more coloury cup; there is no sharp quality season, though the first quarter of the year tends to be best.

The cup is deep copper to red-brown, full and smooth with a mild briskness, light malt and a touch of sweetness; it is the most milk-friendly of the Ceylon districts and makes an excellent everyday breakfast tea. Four minutes with boiling water, milk if you like, and a second steep from leaf grades.

It is sold through the Colombo auction by estate and grade year-round; a good deal of it goes into blends and tea bags, with some estate lots sold on their own. It is not an ageing tea; use it within a year or so of manufacture.

The Ceylon Tea Museum at Hantane, just outside Kandy, is the place to see the island's early machinery and Taylor's story.
history:
The British conquered the Kingdom of Kandy in 1815, and the city remains the capital of the island's Central Province. Its link with the industry is on show at the Ceylon Tea Museum, in the former Hanthana factory built in 1925, about 3 km south of the city.

Little is documented about Kandy as a distinct tea style, which is mostly described in the trade as mid-grown Ceylon.
